utterances.text: Okay, okay. Thank you. So -- I understand that you went to Srebrenica. All I want to know is about when you went. From your evidence, it says that you were wounded in September and that you experienced the attack of the Serbs in November 1992, and that in January 1993 hamlets started to fall in your area, fall to Serb forces. Does -- do I understand you correctly that you actually only went to take up residence in Srebrenica in either January or February or March of 1993? Do I -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No. It was on the 9th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Right. Up until that point, had you visited Srebrenica? From April of 1992 to that point, the 9th of March, 1993, had you visited Srebrenica during that?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just let's go back to Mr. Oric. In 1988 or 1989, indeed 1990, perhaps 1991 as well, do you know if Mr. Oric had a little -- had a Renault, was driving around in a Renault in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a black Mercedes Benz in Srebrenica at all in 1993 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No, I never saw that. I'm not really that familiar with car makes, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That car that you spoke about just a few moments ago that you could see in the clip, did you see that car move around on the day that you -- that you observed all the events you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: The vehicle I mentioned was there from the early morning hours when I went to the front of the municipal building to await the arrival of the APC. That car was parked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to the events in the 6th -- on the 6th of March, 1993. You hadn't had much news from the outside world, I take it. You weren't receiving television broadcasts or radio broadcasts from the outside world. You didn't have any idea what was happening in the rest of Bosnia. Is that fair, a fair comment?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. We didn't have electric power either, so we couldn't follow everything that was happening all over Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were focussed only on saving our own lives. We were an unarmed people trying to stay alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: And to keep our families alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. And therefore, you have no idea at all, would you, of the identities and the names of UNPROFOR personnel working in Bosnia, would you, what they looked like?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: They were different from us. They wore UNPROFOR uniforms and caps and UN insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand that. I have no problem with that. I understand that perfectly well. What I'm saying is: Prior to the 6th of March, you had no idea about the names and personalities and appearances of UNPROFOR soldiers. You didn't know who they were, did you? One was just like the next one. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Well, no. Some were younger, in blue clothes and UN insignia. Only the grey-haired man; people said that was General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When? When did that -- did people say that, on the 6th of March?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes, on the 6th of March in front of the school in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you see the grey-haired man who was pointed out to you as General Morillon for on the 6th of March?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: We were there for several hours around the school when he arrived, when UNPROFOR arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were hundreds, if not thousands, of people milling around the school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes. When I say "thousands," Cerska is a rather large place and a large number of refugees arrived there from Vlasenica municipality. When one hamlet after another began to fall, people poured into Cerska, and all these people then went to Konjevic Polje, so that there were thousands of people. I can't tell you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm -- okay. But I'm concentrating now on that day, the 6th of March, when you say -- well, we could see in the clip. On that particular day there were a number of men walking around in blue -- in blue helmets or hats and soldiers' uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes, there were some people there around the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Where General Morillon was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. That was the first time you heard the name "Morillon," on the 6th of March?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how Mr. Oric came to be there on the 6th of March? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No, I have no information about that. It was by chance that he was there in that crowd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that, that it was by chance? Can you tell us.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Because in that crowd, that large group of people who were there, all gathered around the school, there were UNPROFOR men among us. I saw Naser Oric there on that day, but I don't know when he arrived, what he was doing because we were all focussing on saving our lives since we felt that Konjevic Polje was about to fall. And we weren't relying on anyone. But we understood that UNPROFOR was going to save us. We weren't interested in Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you -- I think in one point in your evidence just a moment ago you mentioned -- yes. You mentioned people gathered around the school in Cerska. Was --

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No, in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. My apologies, Konjevic Polje. Were you -- were the UNPROFOR people inside the school when all the civilians and yourself gathered around the school? Were they inside there? Is that the reason why people gathered around the school?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: They were in front of the school, not in the school, among the crowd of people. And the neighbour I mentioned, Talovic, who was talking with him, the man who had worked in Switzerland and so could speak French, he was talking with General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay. And how long did this sort of -- did this conversation go on for, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Maybe about an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was out the front of the school, not inside the school, not inside the building?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes, in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was General Morillon accompanied by other men in blue helmets and hats?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes. There was a man who was interpreting on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And did General Morillon just talk to this fellow called Talovic?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: At that point in time, he spoke only with Talovic. That's what I observed while the conversation was going on. After that, we left the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You say "we." Do you mean just yourself or all of the refugees who were gathered there, all of the civilians?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: All the civilians, all the civilians. After that, we went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And was that because the men in blue hats and helmets had gone or -- had left and were no longer a centre of attraction for all the civilians?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So General Morillon came along -- you tell me if this is correct, okay? I want to understand you -- make sure I understand you correctly. These soldiers with blue helmets and hats appeared in Konjevic Polje on the 6th of March. A crowd quickly gathered. You were amongst the crowd. General Morillon spoke to this fellow Talovic for about an hour or so. They left, and the crowd dispersed. Is that a fair summary of events?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: After the conversation, UNPROFOR left Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So there's no doubt about it, is there, the only significant -- I should say lengthy conversation that you observed - and you were there for the whole time - was between Morillon and Talovic.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: He didn't tell us anything while he was talking to General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, I --

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: However, after Morillon had left, he only told us to save our families and our own skins.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I understand that. I know that -- I'm not suggesting that you know what the topic of conversation was. But the fact is, isn't it, that the only significant, in the sense lengthy, conversation that any of the soldiers, the blue helmeted soldiers had, was with this guy, this gentleman Mr. Talovic. Right?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No, I didn't observe any other lengthy conversations, apart from that one, which lasted about an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. All right. Now, Mr. Talovic was a local man, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From which village?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Talovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And that -- I take it that's somewhere close to Konjevic Polje and your village of Gusteri. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: It's a hamlet in Cerska. Konjevic Polje is another municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did Mr. Talovic hold any position at the time? Was he, for example, a leader of an armed group or was he a head man in a village? Did he enjoy -- did he have any special sort of status or position at that time, March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you didn't see General Morillon or any of the other soldiers talking to Mr. Oric, did you?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise if I've asked you this before, but I just want to ask you again if -- did you speak to Mr. Oric on that day, the 6th of March, 1993, from what you can recall?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No. I was simply focussing on saving my own skin and on saving my family. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. I'd like to have a look at the clip again, if we could, if Your Honours please, with the yellow hood. I'm sorry I can't remember the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't help you because I don't remember either. MR. DI FAZIO: It was one of the very recent ones. I might have a note of it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P427. Is that correct? I think so. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser. MR. DI FAZIO: And in particular, of course, I'd like to see the clip where we can see -- no, I think this is it, isn't it? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have it on Sanction as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Do Your Honours have a view?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we don't have anything on the screen as of yet. MR. DI FAZIO: No, I don't either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, it's on now, but I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away were you from the group, would you say, when Morillon seemed to be walking around like this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record and before the witness answers, the -- this segment from this video that was run -- that was played, started at 27.46 to 31.15.9. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there is -- this still that the witness is being referred to now is precisely at 31.15.9. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how far away would you have been, about?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I was some 10 to 15 metres away from this crowd of people, from the group of UNPROFOR men we can see on this still.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know who shot this film or from where it was shot, but would you agree with me that if you're down in that crowd it would be pretty hard to see people clearly. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Can we play the film on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Could I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just in order to save time, I would have a question. When we are at this point, had you already realised that Naser Oric was standing there, was he already standing there before Morillon came or was he somehow following Morillon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we were standing there and as General Morillon arrived, I saw Naser up close. He was among the crowd of people, and I'm not sure whether he had arrived with UNPROFOR or not. I'm -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My question is only partly answered so far. Now, when you realised Naser Oric, was he already standing at this point where we see him now before Morillon came, or was he somehow following this group of people, the group of Morillon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, Your Honour, I was part of the crowd when the APC arrived. I don't know whether he was following them or not, but all of a sudden, as the UNPROFOR APC was moving forward through the crowd, in -- it was there that Naser Oric, wearing a yellow hood, appeared in front of the municipality building. I cannot tell you whether he arrived at that particular point in time or later. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: So just to maybe have a clear -- did I -- do I understand you correctly, you had not been aware of Naser Oric being there before Morillon came? Is that a correct assumption of mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Go back a bit, back to the scene with the yellow hood. Yeah, play it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a brief moment - it's only brief - I suggest that the video-clip shows Mr. Oric sticking pretty close to that group of people with the blue helmets and hats. Did you see any such thing on the day, see Mr. Oric pretty close to them for periods of time?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes, he was there close by, some 10 metres, 10 to 15 metres right in front of me, close to the UNPROFOR group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Di Fazio -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is being referred to the -- another portion of the tape, running from 31.15.9 to 31.52.4. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand what you've said, Mr. Guster. What I'm suggesting is that you can see from the -- from the clip that Mr. Oric - albeit for a short period of time - appears to be shadowing or following closely the group. Now, I know it's a long time ago and you may not be able to tell us, but thinking back, did you have any impression of Mr. Oric accompanying or shadowing the group of men with blue hats or helmets?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's probably a hard aspect, and I understand. How far -- about how far is Konjevic Polje from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I don't know the exact amount of kilometres. We went across the woods there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I was with my family with a crowd of people trying to reach Srebrenica. We were walking the entire night. It was only at dawn that we reached Srebrenica. We went across a hilly area, muddy area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: It was that difficult that by the time my children reached Srebrenica, they were already barefoot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a walk of many hours, would you agree, many hours?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a dangerous walk, too. In March of 1993, it wasn't just simply a question of striding off down the road, was it? It was dangerous to move around.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you --

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: The Serbs shelled the group of people on the move from Konjevic Polje to Srebrenica that I was part of. People were getting killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bearing that in mind, weren't you surprised to see Mr. Oric there?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I don't know -- well, I was surprised to see him. He was probably there escorting UNPROFOR. I saw him among the crowd of people and I did not give it any further thought. I was focussed on saving my own skin, that of my family, as were all the other people. I wasn't interested in Naser Oric, or anyone else for that matter. I wasn't even interested in my brother. I was focussed on saving my wife and my children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that, but just one thing. Could you tell the Trial Chamber why you say - what is it that causes you to say - that he was: "Probably escorting UNPROFOR"? Now, why would you have made that comment, do you think?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was escorting them. I did not see him escorting or not. He was there in the crowd, close to the people we can see in the video, and I saw him there for about an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. I -- I understand that, and I hear you clearly. But you said: "He was probably escorting UNPROFOR." Now, you must have some reason for having said that. I -- I just heard you a moment ago, and what I'd like to know is: What possible reason would you have for -- for saying that "He was probably escorting UNPROFOR"? Indeed, what makes you think that it was even a remote possibility that he was escorting UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I mentioned that because he was close to General Morillon's group. That was why I said that, because I thought that perhaps he was escorting UNPROFOR from Konjevic Polje to Srebrenica. But I only saw him there at that spot, where there were many people --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: -- that flocked to the area around the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us this, and I'll leave this point after this. Do you say that he was -- when you say that "He was probably escorting UNPROFOR," was that based on what you saw back then, in March of 1993, or is it based on something else? Is it your memory from March, the 6th of March, 1993, that makes you think that might be a possibility, that he was escorting, Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Not at the time, on the 6th of March, 1993. On that date I said that I was only concerned with saving my children. I wasn't taking interest in anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, let's move to events in Srebrenica. You have described the terrible journey that you had into Srebrenica and of the -- and the events in March that you -- that you saw. You said that you reported to the municipality at one stage to help with the evacuation of the wounded. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness did not say to help with the evacuation of the wounded, but rather that he be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I recall the point when I reported to the municipality to be evacuated as part of the evacuation of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you agree, Mr. -- MR. DI FAZIO: I have just got my note here, I don't have the transcript. I'm sure that what Madam Vidovic says is right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said "applied to the municipality" rather than "reported to the municipality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had your wife and children managed to make it out by that stage?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes. On the 19th of March, 1993, as I said, a convoy arrived with food that we unloaded. I was among the ones unloading it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I've got --

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: And then the next morning I put my wife and children on the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thanks a lot. So you went off to the municipality after they were evacuated. To whom did you put in this application to be evacuated? Who was there at the municipality to -- to hear your application, to entertain it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I don't know the persons there. They all wore civilian clothes. I provided them with my first and last names, to be placed on the list for evacuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know what the name of this -- who these people were or if they had a name? For example, an agency name or some other name identifying them as a body of people? You don't know who they were?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they tell you about the -- about the prospects of evacuation?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: They put me on the list, and I expected to be evacuated any day. And as I've already said, I was there, waiting to be evacuated, every day. Ever since my family had gone on the 19th of March, 1993, I had been waiting in front of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what I want to know about. Did you go and wait in front of the municipality as a result of something that was said to you by those people to whom you -- to whom you applied? Was it them who gave you the idea?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, let me interrupt you for a moment, because looking back at -- I don't know whether this was a question of interpretation or not, but if it was, it needs to be corrected. Page 21, lines 4 and -- that start with line 2. The question was: "Did you stay behind in Srebrenica after you sent your wife away, and what did you do?" And the answer was: "Yes, I stayed behind in Srebrenica. I reported to the municipality to help with the evacuation of the wounded. On the 19th of March, 1993, a convoy carrying food came. On that same day, I went out." So if this is not what he said, it needs to be corrected. If this is what he said, then obviously the whole -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's what my note says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I was following in English and not -- not in Serbo-Croat, so I don't know. Let the witness say what, what --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Shall I ask the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let me try to -- did you hear me reading from what you said, according to the transcript, earlier on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I -- I've understood the discussion well. On the 19th of March, 1993, when I got my wife and children and my mother-in-law onto an UNPROFOR truck, I applied to the municipality for the evacuation of the wounded. Therefore, I applied in the municipality, and then the following two or three days I was standing, together with people from Cerska and Konjevic Polje, from early morning hours all the way till the evening in front of the municipality waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That clears it all. So I think we can proceed from where we -- we had left it, but it was annoying me as it was, so -- your question -- last question was the following, Mr. Di Fazio: "That's what I want to know about. Did you go and wait in front of the municipality as a result of something that was said to you by those people to whom you -- to whom you had applied? Was it them who gave you the idea?" Now this is the question that you need to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't those people who gave us the idea, but rather the group of the wounded who were there, and I was among us, we were told that there was an ongoing evacuation of the wounded and then one -- that one ought to apply to the municipality. That is why I applied and then waited all day long in front of the municipality, because it was the municipality that provided us with information. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you had an expectation or an idea in your head that you could maybe get out, get evacuated, as a result of your wound. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Did they ask you to -- the people at the municipality, did they look at your wound or ask you to go to the hospital to try and make some assessment as to how bad it was?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No. Nobody inspected or examined the wound. The wounded were being evacuated, so that nobody examined them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So there were wounded people being taken out - that's for sure, correct? - at the time you applied to the municipality? There's no doubt in your mind that wounded people were being evacuated?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I don't know. Those of us wounded who were standing there, I -- that's what I can talk about. I don't know about any other groups of wounded being evacuated or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Look, at the time you went off to the municipality to make this application or try and -- to try and get out, to try and be evacuated, did you actually know of -- had you seen, did you actually know of, wounded people being evacuated? Was it something that you knew for certain was happening?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that they were evacuated. I knew only that an evacuation of the wounded was to take place. That was why I applied in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And that information you got from fellow refugees; is that correct? Or you got it from someone in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, we got the information from the municipality. I said that we were standing in front of the municipality in order to be given information concerning the evacuation of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time it's convenient for you. MR. DI FAZIO: This might be a time. Your Honours, I've got a little bit more to go with Mr. Guster --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but we must finish with him today. MR. DI FAZIO: Yeah, I understand that. I understand Your Honour's concerns about that. I'm not saying that, but what I'm saying is I'm going to occupy, I would think, a substantial proportion of the remaining -- I say that for the purposes of the Defence. I know that they've got matters to organise. Sorry about that, but I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: I just need a chunk --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, if Mr. Di Fazio --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, in the meantime, the witness can be escorted out of the courtroom, thank you. We'll have a 30-minute break, Mr. Guster.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Should I start or wait for the witness to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, unless it's something that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. It's simply that obviously time needs to be left for re-examination to finish with the witness, but we would, if at all possible, like, even if it's only a question of 10 or 15 minutes with Professor Bilic, to start with him, and it's partly --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- because he's been in The Hague all week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Really? Already?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and I think psychologically, if not for anything else, just to at least start with his testimony, for his benefit, before the weekend, even if it's only a question of ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you need ten minutes. How much time do you require to make your submissions on the expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I guess it will be less than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Less than ten minutes, so let's make it 20 in all. Out of 45 minutes, how much time do you think you require? MR. DI FAZIO: I would have thought a good part of that, if Your Honours please. It's the last -- 21st of March, and we all know what the witness is going to -- and there's quite a bit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But listen, I'm not trying to stop you, Mr. Di Fazio. Please don't misunderstand me. I'm trying, as usual, to try and accommodate everyone. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now it is that there's someone else sitting, and especially when it's an afternoon sitting coming up for someone else, it means starting late and finishing later. MR. DI FAZIO: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need half an hour? MR. DI FAZIO: Minimum of half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thirty minutes. What we can do is -- I don't know. I don't know. I mean, let's -- let's play it by the ear. I think at this stage I would prefer to -- could I also suggest you think about it a little bit between now and the end of the break. We could call Professor Bilic and I try to explain to him our predicament and whatever and promise him that we will be doing our utmost to get things moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps at the end of the session, if we don't manage to get him on, to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll dedicate five, seven minutes to do that. Let's play it by the ear and see how it works. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's get moving. The accused. Yes, I see Mr. Wubben standing. What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I requested Ms. Patricia Sellers to make a short oral submission regarding the planning and organisation of the rebuttal to update your Trial Chamber. It will be very limited; it's a matter of minutes. We already updated the Defence team of it. And at the same time, Your Honour, I will be happy -- with a view to finalising the witness, I will be more than happy to do my submissions regarding the Trial Chamber expert on Monday morning at the start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Sellers, how long do you expect to take?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's possible less than a minute. Your Honour Brydensholt should have a little more faith in me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm here to make an oral submission under Rule 127 to ask for a variance in the time of the Prosecution following its filing its motion, to request for it to be rescinded -- rebuttal evidence under Rule 85(3). The reason I'm asking for this variance of time is that we have understood between your request and today that there will be some other measures that we must take prior to us being able to provide the names of one or two of the persons, and it would involve going through Rule 70 procedures. The other is that I understand it's a holiday in some parts of former Yugoslavia where we are asking for information to be sent. We discussed this with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What holiday? Now? Today?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What holiday is there in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am unaware of what holiday it is. We have discussed this with Defence counsel, and what the Prosecution would like to propose is that we are more than willing and feel it's our obligation to write a letter to Defence counsel this afternoon disclosing the names, any statements of witnesses that we intend to call whose names we can reveal at this time. We will do full descriptions. We do not want in any way to have the Defence in a position of not knowing information that they could start working on. My understanding was that learned counsel has agreed with this approach and that we will file the motion as required as soon as possible, and I might suggest it will be filed by noon on Tuesday, if not sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed. All right, that's granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll excuse myself from the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how much time -- you think you need about ten minutes for re-examination you said, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So allow about 15 minutes, Mr. Di Fazio. Go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know these events took place on the 21st of March instead of the 20th or the 22nd or the 23rd or, indeed, any other date in March?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: As I mentioned, this man from Konjevic Polje who had a watch on also had dates on his watch, and he showed us the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So other than the fact that this -- a man was wearing a watch and showed you the time, 10.30, you've testified to that earlier this morning, and the date, you wouldn't have had any idea what day it was, would you? Let me rephrase that. You wouldn't have now any idea what day it was.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: That's right. I wouldn't know what day it was, but I do know it was the 21st of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But the only reason you know that, according to what you say, is that the man who was there with you showed you his watch or, alternatively, told you from looking at his watch that it's 10.30 a.m., the 21st of March. Right?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, when the APC arrived, the UNPROFOR APC, the man looked at his watch. I was standing next to him and he showed it to me. It said 10.30 and there was the date there as well, the 21st of March. This was all happening in March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And do you know why he showed you his watch? Can you remember? I mean, it's a remarkable detail to remember some ten years later, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: He showed me to show at what time the APC had arrived so that we could make plans concerning our evacuation to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uh-huh. And how was it going to assist you to know that it was 10.30 a.m. to make plans, to get evacuated to Tuzla? How was that going to help you?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Because in the morning, at around 7.00 a.m., I was in front of the municipality. We were standing around talking, wondering how we could get evacuated to Tuzla. And when we noticed the arrival of the UNPROFOR APC, we were happy that the UNPROFOR vehicle had arrived because we thought it had come to get us. That's why he showed us the watch, so that we would know what time the vehicle had arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And but for the information contained on the watch, that it was the 21st of March, but for that you wouldn't be able to tell us what day these events happened on. Correct? Or perhaps what date, date, these events happened on.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else about the man with the watch? Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: The man next to whom I was standing was a man from Konjevic Polje. His nickname was Burek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can I ask you this: Where were your possessions that -- ready to take with you to Tuzla? Where were they? Did you have a backpack or a little bag, a little satchel, anything at all, a box?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: You saw me on that video with my hands in my pockets, wearing only a shirt. I had nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I understand that times were extremely difficult for you, but you had taken nothing with you, nothing at all? No possessions other than the clothes you had with you. Not even a walking stick to help you with your -- as a result of your wound? What you stood in is what you were going to go to -- is what you were going to travel to Tuzla in?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes, with empty hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I had a wounded leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And what about the other men there, did they have their possessions, any possessions with them, even a bundle of something?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No. The people from Konjevic Polje, they, too, were empty-handed, but they were better dressed than I was, in civilian clothes, because whereas we arrived in Konjevic Polje as refugees from Cerska, they had had time to get dressed as it was winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue to go to the municipality on the 22nd and the 23rd, and on the 24th and the 25th of March, to wait outside the front, waiting to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No, because we had no information about any evacuation to be carried out. So I stayed inside the building. Sometimes when I got bored I would go out in front of the building I was staying in. This was a flat which had no windows and no doors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But why? Why didn't you go there again the next day to wait for the APC to take you to Tuzla? Or indeed the 23rd, the 24th?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Because we hadn't received any information that there would be more evacuations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you make inquiries of the municipality after the events that you've talked about on the 21st? Did you -- let me rephrase that question. You've told us about what you saw on the 21st, and eventually the man who was not well was put in the APC and driven off. Following that, did you go back into the municipality and make any inquiries or try to make any inquiries as to when it might be your turn to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: As I've already said, starting from the early morning, I stood waiting in front of the municipality, together with those other men, waiting to be evacuated. We stood there from early morning until late at night, waiting for the UNPROFOR vehicle to come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it didn't come back. Is that right? You can answer that with a yes or no. It didn't come back?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I want to know is: Why didn't you take up your position the next morning, go back there and wait for the APC to come back?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't have any things. I went out in front of the building I was staying in, after the APC left, to see whether any APCs would pass along the street, but this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I -- that might have happened. But with respect, I don't think you're answering my question. You went there, you say, on the 21st and you've told us about what you saw. You went there because you had hopes or expectations of evacuation through the UN. Now, my question is: You didn't get lucky on the 21st, according to what you said, so why not try again the next day, and the day after that, and the day after that?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I said that I was there on the 21st, and maybe -- or certainly after the 21st for five or six days, I stood there in front of the municipality, but I received no information about any transport of wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's answered your question. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Your Honour. It's really in the spirit of helping. The witness has referred to standing in front of his building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Municipality --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The building where he was staying, and it might be useful just to find out where that is. It might throw some light on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Which building are you referring to? You said that you were standing in front of your building to see whether any APCs would be passing. Which building was this? Where were you staying at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a building to the left of the municipal building. It was a department store. I don't know the name of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We know about it. Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, March of 1993, were there many cars? I don't mean trucks or tractors, vans, motorcycles; I'm talking about cars, saloon cars. Were there many cars driving around Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: As I have told you, at that time while I was there I saw only one car, which was parked in front of the municipality from the early morning. It was parked there the whole morning in front of the municipality. I saw no other cars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that an unusual event, then, to see a car in Srebrenica in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I don't know whether cars were destroyed by the Serbs, but this car was there from the early morning. As I told you, from the early morning that car was there. And as my leg hurt, I leaned against it. So it was a help to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you got, as you speak now, telling us about these events in court here, you've got a clear memory, haven't you - is that what you're saying? - of leaning against the car, looking inside for food? You can remember it in your mind's eye?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes. I was hungry, standing there from the early morning without eating. I looked in through the windows of the car to see if there was any food inside it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Oric the day before the 21st or the day after?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about within a period of about five days either side of the 21st; did you see him then?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the 6th of March, 1993, when he was walking around with a yellow hood, did you see him in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: What I said, the 6th of March, when he was in Konjevic Polje, that's when I saw him. I didn't see him again while I was in Srebrenica. When I went to Srebrenica, I no longer had any occasions to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And how often had you seen General Morillon from the 6th of March, following that? Had you seen him at all?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him except for that time in Konjevic Polje. That was when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the crowd?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: The people I saw, they were very young, and I would still recognise General Morillon if I saw him today, because he was older than all the other men who were with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So the fact is that you laid eyes on General Morillon once from your position in a crowd in Konjevic Polje on the 6th of March, 1993, and you have never seen him since?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings with Mr. Oric at all in 1993 or 1994, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No. As I said, I left Srebrenica in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber the number of men who were present on the 21st of March who had blue helmets on, blue helmets and/or blue hats?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I don't know the precise number, but I do know that several people got out - four, perhaps - and two with blue helmets on accompanied the man in civilian clothes who had one arm missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. But the fact of the matter is you can't tell us precisely how many men were there with blue on their head, either in the form of a helmet or a hat; and that's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I didn't count them. What I was interested in was how to get inside the APC. I didn't care how many of them there were. I tried to get in, and then one UNPROFOR man pulled me out again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And did the -- a crowd of men who -- sorry, not just men but I suppose men and women who were there assembled with you, waiting to be evacuated to Tuzla, also try to get into the APC?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So you're the only one who actually made an attempt to get into it, even though they're all waiting there along with you for exactly the same purpose?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will have only two to three brief questions. Re-examined by Ms. Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Guster, you told us you saw General Morillon at Konjevic Polje. You also told us that you expected the help of the international community. Was General Morillon to you and the people of Konjevic Polje an important, a very important, person?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes. He was important to us because we were told that they were going to save us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Did you take a good look at him?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long were you observing him, approximately?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: For about an hour. For as long as he was talking to my neighbour Talovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any possibility that Morillon or any other person, grey-haired person, was present there when you were observing the sick person, as you put it, being put on a stretcher and into the APC?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: That would not be true. I was there observing the entire event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wish to ask you the following: Before -- how -- how many days or how much time before this particular event did your wife leave the area?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: She left the area on the 9th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a date that you -- that is impressed in your memory?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes. It is still impressed in my memory because that's the date when I saved my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you very near the UNPROFOR men who got out of the UNPROFOR APC?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR soldiers passed by me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to observe them closely?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes. They were very young men who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another intervention for the record. The witness stated that his wife left Srebrenica on the 19th rather than on the 9th, as was entered in the record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you repeat the date when your wife left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes, on the 19th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Judge Brydensholt. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Do you remember what did you exactly do when your wife and children left on the 19th? What did you do the same day?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: From -- or rather, early in the morning I went over to the municipality building and applied to be placed on the list with a view to being evacuated. Therefore, after the evacuation of my family, I went over to apply for evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Could you -- do you remember where did you apply? Was it on -- in an office on the ground floor or on the first floor? How was it, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I don't remember. I was standing at the door to one office where there were people gathered around a desk, and it was there that I got -- applied for the list and I wanted my name to be placed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to correct the record. The witness said "at the entrance," meaning at the entranceway to the building, and it wasn't entered into the record. Perhaps the witness should clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, I think you would agree with what Ms. Vidovic has just stated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was a hospital in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Judge Brydensholt. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Guster, you have told us that you saw Naser Oric the first time on a bus to Belgrade. Did you already talk with him?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No. I didn't talk. Rather, as I said, in 1988 and 1989 we were close to each other but I did not have occasion to talk to him. We were on the bus that all of us were travelling on. There were 50 or 54 of us on the bus. There were people from Cerska, Konjevic Polje. For the most part, the people hailed from Podrinje. That's what I -- what I mean when I say "Cerska."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: If they have been close to each other, then we may conclude, if you are close to somebody, that you also have been in touch with each other by talking with each other. Is that correct, or would you say you saw him but you never had spoken with him?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I said that my friends from Cerska who knew Naser Oric introduced me to him. So it was my friends who introduced me to him. I did not have coffee with Naser Oric. I may have been two or three tables away from where he was seated when we were -- when we stopped on our way, on our journey to Belgrade in a restaurant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And how often did it happen - approximately if you don't know the exact number - did you be on the same bus? Two times, three times, four times, ten times, or what do you think, approximately?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: It was often. Every weekend. From Monday to Friday one worked in Belgrade, and then at the weekend -- or rather, on Friday we travelled from Belgrade to Podrinje. Approximately, we -- our paths crossed some ten times on the bus, but we were not seated at the same table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, coming to the visit of General Morillon in Konjevic Polje, you told us that Morillon talked with your neighbour; I think his name was Talovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And the talk between Morillon and Talovic, did it last for an hour? This talk between Talovic and Morillon, did it last for an hour?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I think it lasted about an hour. I'm not sure -- I don't know exactly how long, but the talk between my neighbour Talovic and General Morillon took about an hour. That was the period during which they talked. I don't know what they talked about. I don't speak any foreign language and I was not able to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: No. I assume that Morillon was a busy man. He had a lot of things to do, and so it's a little bit surprising that he would take time to have a chat with your neighbour in French for almost an hour and people -- other people are standing around and didn't understand anything because they were talking in French.

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that wasn't a chat. This was a conversation about how to save lives which we witnessed, and therefore it was about how to save the lives of those around the school. As I said, later on we were told that we were supposed to save our own skins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones, I saw you standing up at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wasn't sure if it was a comment or a question for the witness, but the witness has answered as if it were a question, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, was Mr. Talovic somehow -- you say mandated by you to have this talk with Morillon or was it more just by chance that Morillon and Talovic had this conversation on the problems with each other?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: It was by coincidence, as Morillon was passing through, that my neighbour Talovic engaged in conversation with him. It actually happened that my neighbour Talovic started speaking French to him, and then General Morillon stopped to talk to him. I don't know what they talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's always a good bait with the French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But did Mr. Talovic report or tell the people around what they had talked about? Did Talovic give you any information on the contents of the talk he had with Morillon?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's turn for a minute to the car in Srebrenica we have been talking about. You arrived there on the morning of the 20th of March, and the car was already there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: On the 21st of March, as I've said, at about 7.00 in the morning the car was already parked in front of the municipal building and remained parked there throughout the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And was it already -- was the car already parked there the day before?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I wasn't able to observe that. I know that it was parked there on that morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And how long -- you say the -- it was parked there in the -- the whole morning. Do you remember approximately the time when the car was driven and moved away from this place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long did it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: How long did it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long did it stay there, starting from the 21st in the morning?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: We were there from early in the morning, as I said, and the car was there parked. We stayed there till the evening, expecting that the UNPROFOR vehicle was to return to evacuate us. And throughout this time, the car remained parked in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Also from the morning but until the evening. You have told us that it was -- that it was parked there until the morning, during the morning. Now, was it more than the morning? Was it also parked there until the afternoon or the evening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't recall where the witness said that it was parked until the morning. If we could be referred to that part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that either, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: He mentioned several times that it was parked during the morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the morning, yeah, but not until the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, my question is: Did you realise when the car was moved away?

utterances.speaker: EJUB GUSTER
utterances.text: I don't remember when the car was moved away. I don't remember. As we were waiting, it became dark and we dispersed. I don't know when the car was removed. I know that, as we were going away, it stayed behind, parked there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge Eser. I thank you, Mr. Guster. We've finished here. You may leave the courtroom now. You will be escorted. I wish to thank you, on behalf of everyone here, for having come over to give testimony. And on behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If -- now -- if someone could help -- please. Let's move because I don't want to keep the staff much longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Professor Bilic, if someone could help her bring in Professor Bilic straight away, straight in. Rather than wait for her, take her -- yeah, but he needs to be escorted in. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please take a seat, Mr. -- Professor Bilic, and good afternoon to you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- and welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, and I'm sure that as a professional man you will understand that things didn't go exactly, precisely as we had planned this morning. We had planned to start with your testimony. I know that you have been here for practically a week already, so you have all our sympathy, and also please accept our apologies for having kept you waiting. We will start with you straight away Monday morning, after we thrash a procedural matter that we have. And we still believe that we will be able to finish with your testimony as planned, by the 26th of the month. So before I ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom again, please do accept our apologies and try to understand that we had another witness and we did our best to try and send him home today, and we were also trying our best to start with you as well, but we did not succeed. Thank you. And I hope you will have a nice weekend here in The Hague. The weather is going to be good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept your justified reasons, and I hope that things will go the way you say they will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Professor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Once more, because yesterday we were all hurried up and I didn't really thank everyone in a proper, decent manner, as I usually try to do. Please, I can't express enough my gratitude to all of you for having stayed over with us more than ten minutes yesterday and practically five minutes later than scheduled today. I do appreciate very much. Yesterday you were instrumental in making it possible for that witness to return home rather than stay here. And today, again, you are instrumental in giving me the opportunity to apologise and explain matters to Professor Bilic. I thank you so much, and I wish this part of the transcript be communicated to the relevant sections in the Tribunal for their acknowledgment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
